label: GPT-6.1 Terra
output:
Peter, I can see why you take that view, especially having run payroll for nine years. You’re right that an informal advance system can become a problem: people can get stuck taking one every month, HR can spend too much time handling requests, and recovering a balance when someone leaves is not guaranteed. Finance is also entitled to know what cash will be needed.

But I disagree that closing the window means people necessarily adjust after one or two pay cycles. We tried almost exactly what you’re suggesting, and we ended up reopening ours.

Brenda, I’m sharing the detail because it may be useful for your meeting on the 18th.

I manage HR at a logistics company of about 340 people, with depots in Embakasi and Changamwe. Most of our staff are drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks. Our old advance arrangement was informal too. Finance pushed for us to close it, making much the same points Peter has made. We stopped advances in February 2025, gave staff two months’ notice and held a financial literacy session with the SACCO.

In the six months that followed, calls to the office from debt collectors and loan apps went from a handful to **61 logged by reception**. That’s calls, not 61 employees, and I can’t say every call was caused by the closure. But the change was hard to ignore. Some apps were calling supervisors whom employees had listed as “referees”, so the collection process was landing at work whether we considered the loan an employee’s private contract or not.

We also saw unplanned absence rise on the two days after month-end. Our fleet manager linked at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers taking time to “sort out” loans. I can’t put every absence down to advances being stopped, but those missed runs were real operational consequences, not just an HR concern.

One case has stayed with me. A loader at Changamwe had six loan apps running at once by the time he came to me, borrowing from one to pay another. It took us four months working with payroll to unwind the situation. I don’t offer that as proof that every employee will end up there. But it does make me cautious about saying people always adjust.

We reopened advances in September 2025, this time under a written policy:

- A maximum of **40% of net pay**.
- No more than one advance per pay cycle.
- The full amount is repaid at the next payroll.
- No fee.
- Requests go through the payroll portal, not through my office.
- Before approving, we check the advance alongside other deductions against the Employment Act’s two-thirds limit on total deductions. The aim is that nobody ends up with nothing at month-end.

That isn’t a magic solution, and the 40% is our limit, not a number every employer must copy. Brenda, you could use it as a starting point with Finance and agree a ceiling that works for your payroll and cash flow. The important difference for us was moving from an informal favour to rules that staff, payroll and Finance could all see.

Since reopening, we’ve had roughly 55–70 requests a month, averaging around KES 9,000. We’ve recovered everything except amounts owed by two leavers, with roughly KES 14,000 written off for the year. So Peter’s point about leavers is a fair one: there is a real loss, and Finance should include it in the calculation. It just needs to be compared with the other costs, not looked at on its own.

That comparison was what changed the conversation for us. There is administration time and there are write-offs. But there is also reception time dealing with collection calls, supervisors being interrupted, HR and payroll time trying to help someone untangle debt, unplanned absence and missed runs. Those costs don’t all appear against the same budget line. Our Finance Manager now defends the scheme himself because the forecast impact is known in advance: there’s a fixed ceiling rather than a surprise.

I agree with you on financial literacy, Peter. It’s worth doing, and I wouldn’t present advances as a substitute for helping people plan or save. But at KES 28,000 a month, knowing how to budget doesn’t necessarily create enough spare cash for an emergency. And a SACCO loan that takes two or three weeks and needs guarantors is not much help when a child is sent home from school over fees on a Tuesday.

Brenda, for the 18th, I’d ask Finance to look at a written, capped scheme alongside the cost of closing it, rather than comparing the current informal arrangement with no cost at all. Your numbers will be different from ours, but you could take in:

- The number and average value of advances over recent months.
- How many employees request them repeatedly, and what has actually been lost when people leave.
- Payroll and HR time spent administering them.
- Any available figures on collection calls, absence, lost production time and supervisor time.
- A proposed cap, one-request-per-cycle limit, full repayment at the next payroll and a clear payroll approval route.

You could also agree with Finance to review the figures after a set period. That gives the MD a way to judge whether the policy is working, including whether repeat use remains a concern.

I wouldn’t defend an open-ended system where people have to come to your office and explain themselves every month. But I also wouldn’t assume that shutting it down removes the need or the cost. In our case, it moved some of both elsewhere—and those other costs were harder to see until we started counting them.
